# SK6061 — A caller-info parameter is followed by an ordinary parameter

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

The compiler only fills a caller-info parameter the caller omitted, so an ordinary parameter declared after one can never be passed positionally without cancelling the substitution it sits in front of.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Design |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, review it |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| Supersedes | S3343 |

## Why

`[CallerMemberName]` is a promise that the caller does not have to say where the call came from. A parameter after it takes that back: to reach the later parameter positionally the caller has to supply the caller-info one too, and the value it then carries is whatever was typed rather than where the call is. The declaration reads as two independent conveniences and behaves as one that disables the other. ⚠ **The failure is silent in both directions** — the caller who wants the later parameter loses the location without a diagnostic, and the caller who wants the location cannot reach the later parameter at all except by name.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
static void Log(string message, [CallerMemberName] string caller = "", int level = 0) { }

// Log("hi", 2) does not compile; Log("hi", "Run", 2) throws the location away.
```

Write:

```csharp
static void Log(string message, int level = 0, [CallerMemberName] string caller = "") { }
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **The shape the issue described does not compile, and establishing that first is what made the rule narrow.** A caller-info attribute on a parameter without a default value is `CS4022` — "may only be applied to parameters with default values" — verified against the compiler rather than assumed, so "a required parameter after a caller-info one" is not a program anyone can write. Everything after an optional parameter is itself optional or `params`, and *that* is the real defect: two optional parameters where the first is filled by the compiler and the second is what the caller wanted.

**A trailing run of caller-info parameters is correct and is never reported.** `(string message, [CallerFilePath] string file = "", [CallerLineNumber] int line = 0)` is the shape the attributes were designed for. The rule fires only where a caller-info parameter is followed by a parameter that carries no caller-info attribute of its own, which is why the fix is a rotation rather than a swap: the whole caller-info run moves to the end together, keeping its internal order.

**Three declarations are declined because reordering them would be wrong rather than unsafe.** An `override`, an explicit or implicit interface implementation, and a `partial` implementation each have a signature fixed by something else in the program; moving a parameter there produces a member that no longer overrides, implements or matches. The finding belongs on the declaration that owns the order, and reporting it on the one that copies it would be reporting a defect at a place that cannot fix it.

⚠ **A `params` parameter is declined outright.** `params` must be last, so the caller-info run has nowhere to go: the only rewrite that satisfies both constraints is the one already written. This is silence rather than a finding without a fix, because a finding a person cannot act on is a finding they learn to skip.

⚠ **The fix is `fixIsSafe: false` and the reason is every existing call site.** Reordering optional parameters silently re-points positional arguments: a caller written as `Log("hi", "x", 2)` still compiles against a reordered signature if the types line up, and now means something else. The rewrite is correct for the declaration and needs the call sites read, which is what review is for. Where it is applied, `SK2141` reports the call sites that were compensating for the old order.

**This rule and `SK2141` are the same defect seen from two ends and cannot double-report.** `SK2141` reports an argument at a call site that restates what the attribute would have supplied; this reports the declaration that made restating it necessary. Neither reads the other's node.
